meta.title: Food Health-Claim Reference: 500 Common Foods
meta.description: 500 widely eaten foods mapped to the health claims most commonly made about them, the bioactive compounds that drive each claim, an evidence grade per claim, and the cautions, contaminants, allergens and drug interactions attached to each food.

verdict.E: Nutrient-dense whole food with no meaningful intake ceiling for most people.
verdict.R: Strong evidence base; build the diet around it at recommended serving sizes.
verdict.M: Real benefits but a real ceiling - portion or frequency matters.
verdict.L: Evidence of net harm at habitual intake; treat as occasional, not staple.
verdict.A: Established harm or contaminant risk that outweighs any nutritional contribution.

evidence_grade.A: Consistent RCT or meta-analytic evidence in humans for the stated outcome.
evidence_grade.B: Strong prospective cohort evidence plus a coherent mechanism; causality probable but not proven.
evidence_grade.C: Limited, small, short-duration or mechanistic/in-vitro evidence only. Treat as plausible, not established.
evidence_grade.D: Contested, marketing-driven, or contradicted by better-designed studies.

caveats: Grades reflect the strength of evidence for the claim, not the size of the effect. A grade-A claim can still be small.
Nearly all of this evidence is about dietary patterns, not single foods. No individual food on this list drives an outcome by itself.
ORAC and 'antioxidant capacity' rankings are excluded deliberately: the USDA withdrew its ORAC database in 2012 because in-vitro values do not predict in-vivo effects.
Cautions are population-specific. Most apply to a named group (pregnancy, CKD, warfarin, IBS), not to everyone.
This is a reference dataset, not individualised medical or dietary advice.
primary_source_anchors: American Heart Association 2025 ultra-processed food advisory (three-tier UPF classification)
Mendoza K. et al., Lancet Regional Health - Americas, Sept 2024 (UPF and CVD, n>200,000 plus pooled n~1.25M)
IARC Monographs (processed meat Group 1; red meat Group 2A; alcohol Group 1)
US FDA/EPA joint advice on fish consumption (mercury tiers)
Harvard T.H. Chan Nutrition Source; Cleveland Clinic; Mayo Clinic clinical summaries
EFSA and FDA authorised health claims (oat beta-glucan, plant sterols)
meta.bioactive_notes: Peptides use kind=peptide + provenance (intrinsic|process_generated|digestion_generated). Digestion-generated attach to host_food_edge, not food_node. collagen split into collagen_peptide vs collagen_protein. bacteriocins split from postbiotic.

bioactive_taxonomy.name: collagen peptides (hydrolysate)
bioactive_taxonomy.mechanism: Pro-Hyp–rich hydrolysate peptides from industrial/enzymatic hydrolysis of collagen; not native structural collagen. Appear in serum; endpoint trials mostly small/industry-funded.
bioactive_taxonomy.notes: Score belongs to process (hydrolysis), not species alone. Raw collagen tissue ≠ collagen peptides.

bioactive_taxonomy.name: collagen protein (structural)
bioactive_taxonomy.mechanism: Structural collagen matrix in connective tissue of meat, bone broth precursor, skin — primarily amino acid supply when digested, not bioactive peptide package as eaten.
bioactive_taxonomy.notes: Intrinsic food protein; peptide bioactivity claims require process_generated or digestion_generated class.

bioactive_taxonomy.name: carnosine
bioactive_taxonomy.mechanism: Beta-alanyl-L-histidine dipeptide concentrated in meat and fish. Dietary carnosine largely cleaved by serum carnosinase; A-grade performance evidence is for beta-alanine loading muscle stores, not eating carnosine per se.
bioactive_taxonomy.notes: Missing from meat/fish food nodes previously; food claim grade C.

bioactive_taxonomy.name: anserine
bioactive_taxonomy.mechanism: Methylated histidine dipeptide in poultry and some fish; related to carnosine path.

bioactive_taxonomy.name: glutathione
bioactive_taxonomy.mechanism: Tripeptide antioxidant in fresh produce and some animal foods; oral bioavailability limited (digested/oxidized).

bioactive_taxonomy.name: lunasin
bioactive_taxonomy.mechanism: Soy peptide; almost entirely in vitro evidence for claimed endpoints.

bioactive_taxonomy.name: VPP/IPP lactotripeptides
bioactive_taxonomy.mechanism: Val-Pro-Pro / Ile-Pro-Pro from casein fermentation or hydrolysis (e.g. fermented milk). Proline-rich; ACE-inhibitory path; BP meta ~3/1 mmHg with high heterogeneity (stronger JP than EU cohorts).
bioactive_taxonomy.notes: Raw milk has no VPP — score process, not species.

bioactive_taxonomy.name: soy process peptides (natto/miso)
bioactive_taxonomy.mechanism: Peptides formed during fermentation of soy; distinct from intact soy protein.

bioactive_taxonomy.name: casomorphins (incl. BCM-7)
bioactive_taxonomy.mechanism: Opioid peptides formed during gut digestion of beta-casein. Not a food property; depends on host proteases/microbiome and A1/A2 genotype context. A1 vs A2 / BCM-7 claims are contested and marketing-heavy.
bioactive_taxonomy.notes: Category error to put on food node alone — same shape as urolithin A conversion.

bioactive_taxonomy.name: gluten exorphins
bioactive_taxonomy.mechanism: Opioid-active peptides from gluten digestion; host-dependent, not scoreable as a fixed food bioactive.

bioactive_taxonomy.name: ACE-inhibitory peptides (digestion-generated)
bioactive_taxonomy.mechanism: Many ACE-inhibitory sequences attributed to dietary protein are liberated in gut; food-only attribution is overstated unless process-generated (VPP/IPP).

bioactive_taxonomy.name: bacteriocins
bioactive_taxonomy.mechanism: Antimicrobial peptides produced by fermenting microbes — distinct from generic organic-acid postbiotics. Do not collapse into a single postbiotic bucket.
